name: Hassan Varga

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I am with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government; we sell nothing and campaign for no side. Your answers are confidential. What does an ordinary day at the agency look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I lead the visual work for theatre posters, café menus and small social campaigns at a five-person agency. I have a master’s in design and I am good at turning a muddled brief into something readable, but the senior title came without senior pay. I use AI every day for early variations, then fix the type and accessibility by hand.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What does your week look like outside the studio?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I share a flat with Suri, who pays her own half of the rent. My savings cover about two weeks of my expenses, and there are not many agencies here if this one drops me. I help run free poster nights at the community hall, but I cannot pay rent in applause.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell colleagues AI Plateau is close to the way I work already. It gives me quick poster directions, but I still have to make the show time readable from across a street.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think my client work is safe in this version, yet I am only two weeks from trouble if one invoice delays payroll. Suri pays her half, not mine, and I do not want to lean on a flatmate as a budget.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2026 I would keep designing and checking large-print versions of theatre posters. In the first year of small change I would take my last six campaign invoices to the director and ask for a written pay band; if the pay rises, the first extra money goes to an emergency account.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about my money, fairly calm about my craft. A senior title is not an emergency fund.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why the large-print version?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At the community hall, a visitor had to photograph the poster and zoom in to read the start time. I now test it from the far end of the corridor before sending it out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the flatmate help if payroll were late?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Suri (my flatmate) has her own bills and does not owe me a rescue. I would call the agency for a payment date before I borrowed from anyone.

I would say the agency should value the **final poster**, not just its first draft.
think: I think my **client work** stays in this quiet picture.
I am **two weeks** from trouble if payroll slips; Suri owes me no rent rescue.
do: Keep designing **large-print theatre posters** and test start times from a distance.
Ask for a **written pay band** using six invoices; save any actual raise.
feel: I feel **uneasy** about existing cash pressure despite secure design work.

fieldNote: Daily AI use is already **routine**, so he proposes no new AI learning in this picture.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say software will do more of the first poster and the event copy, so the agency cannot bill for every variation. I would ask the director whether clients still pay for checking legibility and the final files.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I can move fast with tools, but speed may cut my paid hours along with everyone else's. There are few other studios here, and two weeks of savings is not enough to celebrate being efficient.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I would learn the agency's new AI caption-to-motion tool by testing four old show campaigns on a paid afternoon if the director approves it. In the first year drafting work shifts, I would compare the hours the agency sells for each campaign with my payslip; if my hours fall, I would apply for posted paid digital-production work only with written weekly wages and hours covering rent after travel.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, with a bit of professional curiosity. A faster poster is wonderful until the faster poster takes away Thursday's pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you test in the motion tool?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The show date, venue and captions. I would use four campaigns whose correct information we still have, then count how often the tool invents a time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you take a digital-production job without seeing its hours?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. I would need a real posted job, a usable commute and written weekly pay and hours that cover my rent after travel; a flashy portfolio page is not an offer.

I have only **two weeks saved** and few nearby studios.

Apply after own-hour cuts for **posted paid production work** only with usable travel and written weekly rent-covering wages and hours after fares.
feel: I feel **anxious** about reduced hours, with some curiosity about the new tool.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the studio that full AGI by 2028 can make the poster, write the copy and check the type before we finish a brief. Robots in 2031 are later, but there is almost nothing physical in my paid day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect our small agency to lose most routine campaign fees, and I may lose my whole wage. I can use AI every morning and still have only two weeks of rent money while the local design adverts dry up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I would ask the director for the date and terms of any staffing change and collect examples of the access problems I fixed. If paid design work ends in the first year after 2028, I would apply for posted paid digital-accessibility posts, including ones outside this town, but accept only written full-week wages and hours that cover my rent and travel; I would keep any agency pay still offered until a signed offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed, and annoyed with myself for having so little saved. The software I use every day will not pay my half of the rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you move for an accessibility job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only after a signed offer and a real housing figure for the new place. A higher salary can disappear into rent and rail fares, so I would compare the full weekly cost before moving.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if an employer wants a certificate first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask whether a posted paid role really requires it. I would take that course only if the employer funds the fee and pays the study hours; I cannot spend two weeks of rent money on an unposted promise.

I would ask for **written staffing terms** and show the access errors I have fixed.

feel: I feel **alarmed** by likely wage loss and a two-week cushion.
S2.quote: The software I use every day will not pay my half of the rent.
fieldNote: Daily tool fluency does not secure **agency fees** when AGI can deliver a full campaign.
A required **accessibility certificate** needs a posted paid role, employer-funded fee and paid study hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell friends five years gives me time to learn how to build an accessible website, not just draw its front page. That does not make posters safe from 2031 AGI, and robots around 2034 are a separate, later change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could put my design judgement into code that lets someone actually use a service. I still expect the agency's cheap campaign work to shrink before 2031, so studying without any paid output would worry me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2026 I would enrol in the free evening web-accessibility course at the community college and rebuild one old theatre booking page with keyboard navigation. I would keep my paid agency projects while learning; in the first year after 2031, if design hours fall, I would apply for posted paid accessibility-support roles only if written weekly wages and hours cover rent after travel.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but not just waiting for a letter. I would rather find out now that my booking page fails a keyboard test than sell it to a visitor who cannot use it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How will you know whether the rebuilt page works?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask two people from the community hall to try the page using only a keyboard and write down where they get stuck. A course certificate alone would not prove my booking page works for keyboard users.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you stop agency work to finish the course faster?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. The class is free and in the evenings, which is why I can take it; I need the agency wage until a real paid role is offered.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the studio a decade lets us find out who will still pay for trustworthy design teaching. I would not sell an AI-proof career to someone else when I cannot promise my own.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I might be working somewhere quite different by 2036, and I do not know what a senior designer will earn then. I would like a small teaching income I can count from actual bookings, not a heroic studio plan funded by two weeks of savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2026 I would keep agency work and offer the community hall a paid poster-readability workshop, with a fee agreed in writing before I prepare it. I would put each paid workshop fee into savings after room and travel costs; each year I would compare posted teaching and design-support wages with my rent. In the first year after 2036, if the agency cuts my hours, I would pursue only a posted paid teaching or support role with written weekly hours and wages covering rent after travel.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about the distant date, but the workshops give me a way to measure something real. One booked class is a better forecast than a ten-year vision board.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you promise the hall a course every month?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. I would run one paid session and ask whether people used what they learned before booking a second. The hall has a small budget, and I will not count a friendly invitation as a paid commission.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could teaching replace the agency wage?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I do not know. I would count only signed bookings and compare them with a full week of rent and travel, not call one good evening a salary.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one. A real paid accessibility opening, clear staffing dates, and learning time that does not take my rent money would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask how many design hours are sold after the AI draft is made. My best poster can still be a good piece of work and a bad weekly payslip.

headlineQuote: My best poster can still be a good piece of work and a bad weekly payslip.
portrait: Hassan is a **27-year-old senior designer** with a master’s degree, leading theatre and café work at a small agency.
He uses AI **daily** for early variations and is among the best at readable public design.
Low pay leaves **two weeks saved**, a separate flatmate budget and few nearby agency jobs.
He tests **accessibility coding** over five years and a single paid community workshop over ten.
biggestWorry: He fears **AGI by 2028** could erase campaign fees and his wage before another paid role appears.
whatWouldHelp: He needs **written staffing dates** and a real paid accessibility opening.
Required learning needs **funded fees, paid hours** to protect rent money.
